newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil CenBank sees current account pressure ease.
newsitem.headline: Brazil CenBank sees current account pressure ease.

text.p: Brazil's Central Bank detects signs that pressure on the current account of the balance of payments is abating, especially on the services account, an official said Monday.

Altamir Lopes, head of the bank's economics department, also reaffirmed his faith that the current account gap would be perfectly financeable, despite a $2.147 billion deficit in the balance of payments for the first half of 1997.
"I would say the deficit in the services account will grow very little (in the rest of the year). There is a clear accomodation," Lopes told reporters.
Lopes added there was an accomodation in the trade balance, and interest payments on external debt were stable.

Brazil's current account deficit in the first seven months of the year, including trade in goods and services, stood at $18.901 billion or 4.21 percent of gross domestic product. The deficit in the month of July alone was $3.28 billion.
In the January-July period last year, the deficit was equivalent to 2.28 percent of GDP.
For the 12-month period to the end of July this year, the current account gap stood at 4.35 percent of GDP.

The imbalance in Brazil's external accounts has become a key market concern following speculative attacks on the currencies of Southeast Asian nations, most of which also suffer from high current account deficits.
But the Brazilian government has downplayed fears, saying the deficit was easily financed by inflows of long-term foreign capital, including foreign direct investment.

"I am sure we will finance the whole deficit in the current account," Lopes said. "Although the deficit is high -- no one is saying it isn't -- the rate at which it's growing is not significant and the way you finance it is important."

Lopes said the shortfall in the services account, which reached $14.707 billion in January-June 1997 compared with $10.976 in the same period a year ago, was exacerbated in July by Brazilians travelling overseas during a holiday month.
Gross expenditure on travel in July were $559 million, of which $326 million represented credit card purchases. In July last year, Brazilians spent $469 million on foreign travel.
Gross interest payments on external debt fell marginally to $1.218 billion in July versus $1.222 billion.

Lopes said that even if the trade balance numbers still looked ugly -- Brazil posted an $811 million trade gap last month -- the financing of the trade deficit was becoming healthier due to new import financing rules introduced in March.
He said that 32 percent of all imports in July were being financed with maturities of over one year.
Likewise, inflows of long-term capital through privatizations and other investments were gathering pace.
In July, $1.418 billion in foreign direct investment flowed into the Central Bank's books. Of that, only $574 million was related to privatizations.
"The amount of money being invested outside the privatization program is pretty significant," Lopes said.
